title: Unto us a child (Isaiah 9:2–7)
hookLine: the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light

lines: A STRING OF NAMES, HAMMERED OUT.
cards: In December, in concert halls and churches in many countries, a choir waits for a particular chorus. The violins start running, light and quick.
Then the whole choir lands, all together, on a string of names, hammered out one at a time. Handel wrote it in London, and it was first heard in Dublin in 1742. But the words weren't his.
They come from the prophet Isaiah, written more than seven centuries before Jesus, to a kingdom with an army on its border.

teach.b: Isaiah's world was dark in a literal way. The Assyrian empire was on the march, and the northern lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, up around the Sea of Galilee, were among the first to be overrun.

Into that, Isaiah says, in the King James Bible: "The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined." Notice the tense.

teach.h: HAVE SEEN: SPOKEN AS IF DONE.
teach.b: Have seen: the rescue spoken of as if it's already happened.

Then he names the light: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace."
Not a general. Not a weapon. A baby.
The soldiers' boots, Isaiah says, will be burned as fuel for the fire, and this child's peace will have no end, on the throne of David. Who is the child? Here readers differ.
Many Jewish readers have understood it as a royal child of Isaiah's own time, often King Hezekiah, or as a future king of David's line. Christians, from the Gospels on, read it as Jesus.
Matthew's Gospel quotes this very passage when Jesus begins preaching in Galilee, the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, the first place the darkness fell.

teach.h: THE PEOPLE THAT WALKED IN DARKNESS HAVE SEEN A GREAT LIGHT.
teach.b: For Christians, the light rose exactly where the shadow had begun. That's why these words come back every Christmas: a child, given, into a dark place.

how: Isaiah 9:2–7 is one of the most common readings at Christmas services, including the traditional service of lessons and carols, and many Christians light candles through Advent while waiting for Christmas.

o: a title for the wisest judge in a royal court
a name Isaiah gives the child born in darkness
a nickname Handel gave his favorite singer

games.q: what's inside the prophecy — tap the pairs.
p: the rescue spoken as if done

s: Handel wrote the words of For unto us a child is born
the words are Isaiah's, written more than seven centuries before Jesus.
Matthew quotes this passage when Jesus begins preaching in Galilee
Matthew 4:15–16, in the land of Zebulun and Naphtali.
Jewish and Christian readers agree on who the child is
many Jewish readers see a king of Isaiah's day, often Hezekiah; Christians read it as Jesus.

games.q: your land is overrun, and the army is still coming. a prophet says rescue is on the way. what does he say it is?
o: a great general with a larger army.
a wall too high to climb.
games.why: "for unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given." not a weapon. a baby, whose peace has no end.

practice: If you can, light a real candle and set it in front of you; if not, picture one clearly, and notice how small the flame is, and how much of the room it changes.
Then think of one dark place you know about right now, a family going through something, a city in the news, a corner of your own life, and hold the flame and that place together in your mind.
If you pray, you can pray for that place by name.

wordCard.voice: Wonderful Counsellor. One of the names Isaiah gives the child born for a people in darkness, a promise Christians read as the birth of Jesus.

orig.note: Hebrew: for a child has been born to us.

carryVoice: Your line: a great light. Even a small flame changes a room. See you tomorrow.
